title: Clocks & Ordering
subtitle: Watch two replicas disagree about which write came last, then fix it with logical clocks.
learn: Why wall clocks on different machines never agree exactly, and what NTP can and cannot fix
How last-write-wins can silently throw away the newer write
What happens-before means and how to tell ordered events from concurrent ones
How Lamport timestamps and vector clocks capture causality
Why hybrid logical clocks pair physical time with a counter

steps.title: Which write came last?
steps.body: A shopping-cart value is stored on two replicas. Client 1 sets it to "red" through Replica A. Fifty milliseconds later Client 2 reads "red", changes it to "blue", and writes through Replica B. Blue is clearly the newer intent. Can the system work that out by comparing timestamps?
steps.idea: Deciding what happened after what is the core problem; timestamps are only one way to answer it.
steps.caption: Two clients, two replicas, one value.

steps.title: Clocks drift and disagree
steps.body: Each machine counts time with a quartz crystal. A typical crystal is off by 10 to 100 parts per million, which is up to 8 seconds a day if left alone. So two servers always show slightly different times. Here Replica B's clock runs 120 ms behind Replica A's. That gap is called clock skew.
steps.idea: There is no single 'now' across machines; every clock is a slightly wrong local guess.
steps.caption: Replica B's clock is 120 ms behind A.

steps.title: NTP shrinks skew, never removes it
steps.body: NTP (Network Time Protocol) lets a machine ask a time server for the time, estimate the network delay, and nudge its own clock. Over the public internet it typically gets within a few to a few tens of milliseconds. Tuned datacenter setups using chrony or PTP can reach well under a millisecond. Errors still come back: a missed sync, a VM pause, or a leap second can jump a clock.
steps.idea: Synchronized clocks are close, not equal, so a timestamp comparison smaller than the error margin means nothing.
steps.caption: Replicas sync to NTP; skew drops to about 5 ms.

steps.title: Last-write-wins loses data
steps.body: Suppose the sync lapsed and B is 120 ms behind again. Replica A stamps red at 10:00:00.100. Fifty ms later, B stamps blue with its slow clock: 10:00:00.030. The merge rule last-write-wins (LWW) keeps the biggest timestamp, so red wins and the newer blue write is silently discarded. No error, no log, just a lost update.
steps.idea: LWW trusts wall clocks to order events, so skew larger than the gap between writes makes it drop the real latest write.
steps.caption: Blue is dropped because B's clock is behind.

steps.title: Happens-before
steps.body: Instead of asking what time it was, ask what could have influenced what. Event X happens before Y if they run on the same machine with X first, or X sends a message that Y receives, or a chain of such links connects them. If neither happens before the other, they are concurrent: neither could have known about the other. Red then blue is ordered because Client 2 read red first.
steps.idea: Causality, not wall-clock time, defines order: A happens-before B only if information could have flowed from A to B.
steps.caption: Client 2's write depends on red; it is causally later.

steps.title: Lamport timestamps
steps.body: Leslie Lamport's trick needs no clocks at all. Each node keeps a counter. It adds 1 for every local event and attaches the counter to every message. On receiving a message the node sets its counter to max(its own, the message's) + 1. So if X happens before Y, X's number is smaller. The reverse does not hold: a smaller number does not prove causality.
steps.idea: A Lamport clock gives a total order consistent with causality, but cannot tell concurrent events from ordered ones.
steps.caption: Counters ride on messages; B jumps past A's value.

steps.title: Vector clocks spot concurrency
steps.body: A vector clock keeps one counter per node. Red is written at A as [A1, B0]. B receives it and writes blue as [A1, B1]. Every entry is at least as large, so blue replaces red safely. But if A also takes a different write, giving [A2, B0], that and [A1, B1] are incomparable. The system keeps both as siblings for the app or a merge rule to resolve. Dynamo-style stores like Riak use this.
steps.idea: Comparing vectors tells you three things: older, newer, or truly concurrent. The cost is a vector that grows with the number of writers.
steps.caption: Ordered writes replace; concurrent ones are kept.

steps.title: Hybrid logical clocks
steps.body: Lamport and vector values mean nothing to a human and cannot answer 'show me data from 9am'. A hybrid logical clock (HLC) stores the physical time plus a small counter. It follows the wall clock closely, but if a message arrives from the future, it bumps the counter instead of going backwards. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use HLCs. Google Spanner takes another route: its TrueTime API reports an uncertainty interval, and commits wait it out, typically a few milliseconds.
steps.idea: HLCs keep causal ordering and stay close to real time, at the cost of bounded, not zero, dependence on synchronized clocks.
steps.caption: Timestamps carry time plus a tiebreak counter.

steps.title: Pick the right clock
steps.body: Wall clocks drift, and NTP only narrows the error, so comparing timestamps from different machines can reorder events and let LWW lose data. Lamport clocks give a causal-consistent order. Vector clocks also detect concurrency. HLCs mix both ideas with readable time. How to merge concurrent writes is left to the conflict-resolution lesson.
steps.idea: Use time for humans and logs, and use causality tracking when correctness depends on order.
steps.caption: Causality tracking keeps both writes visible.

quiz.q: Replica A and B are synced by NTP to within about 20 ms. Two writes to the same key happen 5 ms apart on different replicas. What can a timestamp comparison tell you?
options: Which write is newer, because NTP is accurate
Which write is newer, as long as the clocks are in the same timezone
Nothing reliable, since the gap is smaller than the clock error
That the writes are concurrent
quiz.why: Skew of 20 ms is larger than the 5 ms gap, so either replica's stamp could be ahead. The comparison is within the noise and cannot be trusted.

quiz.q: Last-write-wins is used to merge two replicas. Which scenario most clearly causes silent data loss?
options: Both replicas have exactly the same clock
The replica that took the later write has a clock running behind the other
The writes are to different keys
The network is slow but all messages arrive
quiz.why: A later write stamped by a slow clock gets a smaller timestamp, so the merge discards it even though it was the latest in real time.

quiz.q: Two vector clocks are [A:3, B:1] and [A:2, B:2]. What is their relationship?
options: The first is older
The second is older
They are identical
They are concurrent
quiz.why: Neither vector is greater than or equal in every entry: A is higher in the first, B is higher in the second. So neither write saw the other.

quiz.q: Event X has Lamport timestamp 7 and event Y has Lamport timestamp 9. What can you conclude?
options: X happened before Y
Y cannot have happened before X
X and Y are concurrent
Y happened before X
quiz.why: If Y happened before X, then Y's timestamp would be smaller. So Y cannot precede X, but X may still be concurrent with Y, which is why 'X happened before Y' is not guaranteed.

quiz.q: Why would a database choose a hybrid logical clock over a plain Lamport clock?
options: HLCs need no counter
HLC timestamps stay close to real time, so you can query by time and still respect causality
HLCs eliminate clock skew
HLCs detect concurrent writes like vector clocks
quiz.why: An HLC pairs physical time with a counter: readable, near wall-clock, and causality-safe. It does not remove skew or give per-node concurrency detection.

cheatsheet.def: The difference between two machines' clocks at the same real instant. Always non-zero; NTP keeps it to roughly ms, not zero.
How fast a clock gains or loses time. Cheap crystals drift tens of parts per million, several seconds per day if unsynced.
X → Y if X precedes Y on one node, or X is a send whose receive is Y, or by chaining. Otherwise the events are concurrent.
A counter bumped per event and set to max(local, received) + 1 on receive. If X → Y then L(X) < L(Y); the reverse is not guaranteed.
One counter per node. Compare entry-wise to find older, newer, or concurrent. Grows with the number of writers.
Physical time plus a logical counter. Stays near wall-clock time and never goes backwards. Used by CockroachDB, YugabyteDB.
Keeps the highest timestamp. Simple, but loses updates under skew or true concurrency. Fine for idempotent overwrites like caches.
